title: The Psalms and Isaiah Name the Son God
english: “Creator,” and “Sovereign,” and “of his peace there is no bound” (Isaiah 9:7), and “Saviour,” and “Christ is all in all” (Colossians 3:11), and “blessed for ever” (Romans 9:5); and that “great is the mystery of godliness” (1 Timothy 3:16), plainly the mystery of the Christians, among whom Christ is hymned as uncreated God; and that by his own Godhead “he acquires the people,” because he is of one substance with the Father.

Such, then, is what the saints we shall now mention say on these matters, the saints to whom God, as Psalm 16 says, “made known the ways of life” (Psalm 16:11). David in Psalm 7 prays: “Arise, O Lord my God, by the command you gave, and an assembly of peoples shall surround you; and for its sake return on high” (Psalm 7:6-7). You see that the prophet knows him as Lord and God, and entreats him when he says “Arise”: arise to your ineffable incarnation, in the way you marked out beforehand when you said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). For by “for its sake” he means the salvation that comes to us from it: “The nations will surround you by faith; and you, return without separation to the place from which you came.”

And in Psalm 47: “The Lord is a great God, and a great King over all the earth” (Psalm 47:2). And in Psalm 50: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, out of Zion is the splendour of his beauty; God will come openly” (Psalm 50:1-3). And in Psalm 68: “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered” (Psalm 68:1), and “Make a way for him who rides upon the west; the Lord is his name” (Psalm 68:4). And in Psalm 82: “Arise, O God, judge the earth” (Psalm 82:8).

Observe how each word kindles his glory and is enough to persuade us that he is of the substance of the Father’s unity. Observe, too, that the writer of great things calls God the one who was laid in the tomb not without life, so that he might save, together with the living, those also who had departed from human affairs; and he prophesies that he rises from the grave to judge those who, after a kindness so great and so vast, set their minds on earthly things. Know that by “the west” he means the last times; for it was in them that he came openly into this visible world.

And in Psalm 77: “Your way is in the holy place. Who is a great God like our God? You are the God who alone works wonders” (Psalm 77:13-14). Here too he extols God the Word made flesh, who loved to linger in the Jewish temple, and taught there, and worked wonders.

And in Psalm 118: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the Lord is a great God, and he has appeared to us” (Psalm 118:26-27). If it is with good reason that the Lord who appeared to us is, in the prophet, “a great God” and “blessed” (that is, glorified), and “great King” and “only worker of wonders,” and this is the Son, then it is without reason that the heretics suspect him of being less than his own Father. For it is not possible for one and the same being, in truth, to hold the first place according to the prophecy and the second according to them.

If we inquire of the same psalmist, we shall learn that he knows the Son, like the Father, to be the God of our forefathers. For in Psalm 47 he has cried out: “God reigns over the nations; God sits upon his holy throne. The rulers of the peoples were gathered with the God of Abraham” (Psalm 47:8-9). They assembled together with God made man, of whom it is sung in Psalm 2: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples plot vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers were gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm 2:1-2).

Isaiah cries out that he, like God the Father, is beyond compare: “From of old we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen, a God besides you” (Isaiah 64:4). For we have seen no other God than the one born of the Virgin Mary in the saving incarnation; nor have we heard any other, except the one to whom God the Father bore witness: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17). And again, as was said before: “A child was born to us, a son also was given, whose rule is upon his shoulder; and his name is called Mighty God, Sovereign, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come” (Isaiah 9:6). And after other words he adds: “And of his peace there is no bound” (Isaiah 9:7).

The Son of God, he means, having become man, was born a child and was given to us, himself bearing upon his shoulder the rule, the very beginning, of this his birth here below. That is, he is himself his own beginning, in that he was born of a virgin without passion and was ineffably made flesh from her, while no union with a man supplied his beginning. And his name is “Mighty God, Sovereign.” He did not say “subject to authority”; he disclosed his nature, his power, his sovereign authority. Knowing this name, David sings: “Let them know that your name …

title: The Great God and Saviour: Baruch, Titus and Colossians
english: … is Lord; you alone are Most High over all the earth” (Psalm 83:18). He said “alone” because of the one Godhead. He called him Father of the age to come, though he is the Creator of the past ages as well, because it was from the time of the dispensation that he became widely known to men. So he called him Father of a created nature, not of an uncreated one; for the Father of the uncreated and consubstantial Son is one. And pointing to the immeasurable greatness of his Godhead, he said: “Of his peace there is no bound” (Isaiah 9:7).

Jeremiah too, or Baruch (for the two have one book), speaks of him in solemn words: “This is our God; no other shall be compared with him. He found out every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel whom he loved. Afterwards he was seen on earth and lived among men” (Baruch 3:35-37). If, then, it is not understood in a way worthy of God, that the passage before us was spoken so because both the ineffable hypostases have the same Godhead, it remains to fall into godlessness and say that the God and Father who begot him is not our God and is not to be compared with his Son.

So the argument of those who slander God the Word as lesser and a subordinate has fallen and vanished altogether. For how could another be beyond compare with God, he “with whom no other shall be compared”? And again: “Let the gods who did not make the heaven and the earth perish from the earth. The Lord, who made the heavens by understanding, he is the living and true God” (Jeremiah 10:10-12). This is said because no other Godhead is true except that of the genuine Son of God, through whom and from whom the heavens too were brought forth, together with the whole world.

And Paul, the most eminent of men, keeping the same sequence as the prophets, gives the words that befit him. To Titus he writes: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works” (Titus 2:13-14). By declaring “of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ,” he shows that the Son does not stand second in substance, and that he is without beginning in relation to the great God the Father. Indeed, one can see it from what is plain on the surface: if the Son is small, how will the Father be great? If there “was a time when he was not” for God the Word, there was a time when the name of Father did not exist. May we be pardoned for daring to say such things; we say them because of the senselessness of others. “For reverence,” as they say, “is a fine habit for those who practise it.”

By saying “who gave himself for us, to purify for himself a people of his own,” and not “to purify a people for another,” he brings out something further, in keeping with what has been mentioned. For it signifies that he has received as his own the one Godhead, self-determining and good, the cause of all things. To die for one’s own handiwork, if one may put it so, belongs to a creator and not to a creature; and to acquire the people for himself belongs to a beloved Son whose Godhead and kingdom are no different from the Father’s.

Carrying the argument on, this great and true interpreter sets out to show that he is at once a loving and saving God, and at once that it was by prevailing upon himself, and not by yielding to a higher Godhead, that he came to be with us as one of us, without change and without sin. He says: “When indeed the kindness and love for mankind of God our Saviour appeared, not by works which we had done, but according to his great mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:4-5).

To the Colossians he both gives rebuke and lays the foundation of the very first theology concerning him, writing, as was said already in the chapter “On the Consubstantial”: “Why according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ Jesus? For in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily” (Colossians 2:8-9), that is, in substance. For he is by nature fullness itself, being in his substance the Father’s Godhead. “For he did not count it robbery to be equal with God” (Philippians 2:6). But we, through his goodness, received grace from the fullness, a grace which by nature, as servants, we did not have. So John says: “And from his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace” (John 1:16); that is, the grace of rebirth in place of the grace we cast away when we set aside the first ordinance, given about the one tree. “For no longer,” …

title: God Manifest in the Flesh: Paul, Thomas, John and Jude
english: … he says, “are you under law, but under grace” (Romans 6:14). And again: “For in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to him” (Colossians 1:19-20).

This too follows from what went before. For the Father is by nature in the Son, and the Son in the Father, just as everything akin stands, in a way, inseparable from what is akin to it, even if it is divided in hypostasis. So the saying in the passage under discussion is fine as well, though it is not very deep, yet not easy for everyone to take in at a glance: “through him and to him to reconcile all things.” Thus the word spoken of the Father, “from whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6), fits the Son too, if indeed both what has now been said and the words “in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead” (Colossians 2:9) hold sound.

Writing to Timothy as well, Paul spoke of him as God in the highest degree, and from both expressions he taught that in his Godhead he is not outside the Father’s nature. For he spoke thus: “Confessedly great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16). For this Maker and Benefactor of all, who was not yet plainly manifest to all, was found manifest when, for the salvation of all, he willingly became as one of all.

Hence “he was justified in the Spirit”: that is, he was declared, or rather confirmed, to be true God even by those who had not known him in the time before. And this, he says, was not without testing, but by the very movement of our soul, as common usage puts it: “So-and-so was justified as truly the son of such a one,” when he has furnished proof of his descent; and again, “So-and-so was justified in governing well.”

And so that the account may seem more persuasive, he holds that he was seen by angels too, to whom, because of his divine infinity and formlessness, he had been invisible before that time, like “the only invisible God” (1 Timothy 1:17); and that he was hymned by them: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will among men” (Luke 2:14). He holds that he was preached and believed on in this whole world, because he who shone forth timelessly from the ineffable light was ineffably born of the ever-virgin in later times, out of love for mankind, and showed forth in himself all that is the Father’s; and that he went up to the One who embraces all things, in the glory in which he always was with God.

Worthy of belief, too, is the very one of whom we speak, when he bears witness to his own Godhead and lordship. In Matthew he says to the devil, “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matthew 4:7); in John he says to the apostles, “You call me the Lord and the Teacher, and you say well, for so I am” (John 13:13). And Thomas, when he touched the marks of the nails, which the Saviour in his love for mankind bore from us for our sake, was not troubled, nor did he lower his supreme estimate of him. For he knew that it belonged only to the sovereign nature, infinite in power and supremely good, and certainly not to a created one, not only to suffer for its own creatures, but also to bestow the salvation we call universal and general, and that for ever. Therefore, taking still greater courage from this, he offers him firm faith in return and cries out: “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28).

In the catholic epistles too, as was said before, they wrote of the Son as God equally with the Father and in the same words. John, the great among theologians, says: “And we know that the Word of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God; and we are in the true one, in the Son of God, Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). Do not seek, he means, a God other in substance than the Son of God. For I have twice told you that “true” belongs to him: he is both “true Son” and “true God,” who has given understanding to those worthy to receive it; so that you may know that he was truly begotten and is truly consubstantial with the God who begot him.

Jude, one of the twelve, defined him as sole Owner, as one who has received for his lot the Father’s Godhead, which is over all and through all and in all. He writes somewhere in this way to those everywhere: “For certain men have crept in, who long ago were marked out for this judgment, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into licentiousness and denying the only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (Jude 4). And Peter too, the chief among the apostles, is shown in the Acts saying: “The word which he sent to the sons of Israel, preaching peace through Jesus Christ: he is of all …
